div.head: Wl art 8.2
div.ab: Et qui iuste uenire deberent et uenire noluerint, semel summoneantur; et si secundo uenire noluerint, accipiatur unus bos, et summoneantur tertio; et si non tertio uenerint, accipiatur alius bos.
Et qui iuste venire deberent et venire noluerint, semel summo[n]eantur; et si secundo venire noluerint, accipiatur unus bos et summo[n]eantur tertio; et si non tertio venerint, accipiatur alius bos.

And those who are legally required to appear before them, and refuse to do so, shall be summoned once; and if they refuse to appear on the second summons, an ox shall be confiscated and they shall be summoned a third time; and if they do not come on the third summons, another ox shall be confiscated.
div.note: Added October 2026 from Robertson pp. 240–241 (text and translation); Liebermann’s text added from Gesetze I p. 488, October 2026 (two independent readings of the page images)

Hier bis 8, 3 wird nur die zum Prozess trotz Vorladung (s. d. Gl 7. a) ausbleibende verklagte Partei gemeint.—Ein Ochs (s. d. Gl 5) wird auch sonst Säumigen fortgenommen als Strafgeldfixum; s. d. 9. Wahrscheinlich wird damit Ungehorsam (s. d. 25—c) gegen das Hundred (s. d. 18b. c) gebüsst. Es passt der Betrag aber nicht für die Grafschaft; diese ist vielleicht nur durch einen Nachgedanken mit jenem verbunden, wie zweimal in Leis Wl 43f., wo dieselbe Cnutstelle benutzt wird

From here to 8, 3 only the accused party who fails to appear for the suit despite summons (see that word in Gl 7. a) is meant.—An ox (see that word in Gl 5) is taken from defaulters elsewhere too, as a fixed fine; see that word 9. This probably punishes disobedience (see that word 25—c) towards the hundred (see that word 18b. c). But the amount does not fit the shire; this has perhaps been linked with the hundred only as an afterthought, as twice in Leis Wl 43f., where the same passage of Cnut is used
